---
title: "Setting up a cluster for geospatial R"
subtitle: "Written for whoever administers the workspace, not for the person using it"
---

If you have arrived here from another page, this one is not addressed to you. Pass it on.

This was verified in a test workspace, and in yours much of it may already be done. It addresses **DBR 18.1**; where a detail is runtime-specific that is called out, because several of these answers have changed.

## What is missing

The stock runtime image ships no GDAL, GEOS or PROJ, so `install.packages("sf")` fails while configuring. That single fact is the whole reason this page exists.

The person who sent you here cannot fix it. System libraries need root and need to be present on every machine in the cluster, so no amount of work in an R session gets there. The error surfaces in R, which is why it is usually reported to you as an R problem.

## Two separate layers

Conflating them costs a week. The system layer needs an init script and root privileges. The R layer needs a package repository and a library path. Fixing either one alone leaves the same symptom, which is precisely why the two get conflated.

So expect to do both, and expect the first to look like it did nothing until the second is also done.

## Why an init script

It runs on every node. An interactive install touches only the driver.

That is the whole argument, and it is worth being firm about, because an interactive install appears to work. Someone tries it by hand, `sf` loads, the problem looks solved, and then it fails inside a worker where the libraries were never installed. An init script is the only form that reaches every machine.

## Build times

Point the install at a binary repository and it will still compile from source, taking about fifteen minutes per node instead of seconds. There are two reasons, and the second is the one nobody guesses.

The first is ordinary: binaries are keyed to both the Linux distribution and the R minor version, so the generic repository URL serves sources unless you use the distribution-specific path.

The second is that the repository decides whether to serve binaries by reading the `R/<version>` token at the front of the request's user agent. An interactive R session sends it. `Rscript` does not, and an init script is exactly that case. So you get sources: same command, same repository, correct URL, and the only symptom is the fifteen minutes.

Set the user agent explicitly to fix it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
options(HTTPUserAgent = sprintf(
  "R/%s R (%s)",
  getRversion(),
  paste(getRversion(), R.version$platform, R.version$arch, R.version$os)
))
```

Worth stating carefully, because pointing at the distribution-specific URL is still necessary and is not wrong, merely incomplete. Fixing only the URL changes nothing observable, which makes correct advice look wrong when it is half right.

## Version constraints found in practice

This section is runtime-specific, and the answer has changed.

On older runtimes, `terra` needed pinning against the image's GDAL version, and `Rcpp` needed upgrading before `units` would install. On DBR 18 neither is necessary.

Two things follow. A script carrying those constraints forward keeps pins that no longer apply, which leaves packages missing or recompiling at every start, so the runtime version and the setup script are one decision rather than two: moving the runtime means revising the script.

And if you are going to quote measured library versions to anyone, pin the runtime to a specific version rather than a rolling alias. An alias moves, and the GDAL or GEOS version you documented silently stops matching.

## Pay it once

The durable arrangement, and the one worth the extra half hour:

1. Build the packages to local disk on a cluster with the system libraries present.
2. Copy the resulting library tree to a Unity Catalog volume.
3. Have users prepend that path to `.libPaths()`.

Any later cluster with the same R version and image can reuse the tree, so the build cost is paid once rather than at every cluster start. It has been verified working inside a `spark_apply()` worker, which matters: a fix that only works on the driver does not help anyone doing distributed work.

Tell the person who sent you here that the volume exists and what its path is. From their side it is one line, and they have no way to discover it.

## Why installs vanish

Which is why the volume above is the durable fix and an install is not.

An install goes away. Users read that as the upgrade having failed, run it again, get the same result, and eventually ask you. The library on a volume is the thing that stops the cycle.
